# Discussion

## What Are the NAPs About?

The structural topic model reveals what forty-seven National Adaptation Plans actually contain—and perhaps more significantly, what they do not. Eight topics organize the entire corpus, yet their distribution tells a striking story. A single topic, characterized by terms like "mainstream," "learn," "agreement," "pari," and "progress," commands 30.8% of the discourse. This procedural and planning vocabulary appears meaningfully in 45 of 47 documents. Meanwhile, topics addressing actual climate impacts—sea rise (9.5%), cyclones (9.4%), mountain ecosystems (8.4%)—remain fragmented and geographically confined. What explains this extraordinary imbalance between process and substance?

From an institutional perspective, the content patterns validate decades of climate governance architecture. The dominance of Topic 8 demonstrates that countries have successfully internalized adaptation as a governance challenge requiring standardized frameworks. The ubiquity of "mainstream" signals that adaptation cannot remain siloed in environment ministries but must permeate all government functions. The prominence of "agreement" and "pari" (Paris Agreement) shows alignment with global climate architecture, while "learn" and "progress" indicate adoption of adaptive management approaches.

Consider the distribution across income levels. High-income countries show the highest dominance values (0.657), suggesting they have most fully absorbed these frameworks. That Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina share mountain-focused topics (Topic 3) while Philippines and Tonga emphasize cyclones (Topic 2) indicates appropriate localization within standardized frameworks. The institutional reading sees countries successfully balancing global coordination with local specificity.

Topic 5's emphasis on "offic," "climate-resili," "medium," "secretariat," and "depart" (11.7% of corpus) reinforces this interpretation. Countries recognize that adaptation requires institutional infrastructure—offices to coordinate, departments to implement, secretariats to monitor. That Bhutan and Nepal lead in this organizational emphasis reflects their understanding that institutional capacity precedes effective adaptation. The prevalence of "medium" suggests appropriate attention to temporal planning horizons.

Even Topic 1's vocabulary—"ment," "tion," "napa," "percent," "pro"—though seemingly fragmented, reveals systematic attention to implementation, national adaptation programme approaches, and quantification. Chad and Mozambique's leadership here indicates that even least developed countries engage with systematic planning frameworks.

Yet examining what dominates reveals what is marginalized. The structural perspective notices immediately what is absent from these eight topics: rights, reparations, historical responsibility, loss and damage, sovereignty, land tenure, displacement. These absences are not random but systematic, revealing how power shapes discourse.

Consider how Topic 8's dominance operates. When 30.8% of discourse focuses on "mainstream" and "progress," this crowds out discussion of why vulnerability exists. Ferguson's [@ferguson1994] anti-politics machine functions precisely through such technical discourse—rendering political questions about causation and responsibility into managerial problems about coordination and learning. Countries must demonstrate fluency in mainstreaming not because it addresses climate impacts but because it unlocks climate finance.

The correlation between income and discourse patterns exposes these dynamics empirically. The gradient from high-income (0.657 dominance) to low-income (0.518) countries reveals that wealth purchases discourse autonomy. Poorer countries facing the most severe impacts have the least freedom to define their adaptation needs. They must adopt the procedural language of donors—the very language that obscures the structural causes of their vulnerability.

Topic 5's institutional focus deserves scrutiny. The emphasis on offices and departments assumes functioning states capable of complex coordination. Yet as Scott [@scott1998] demonstrates, such institutional blueprints often fail to recognize how things actually work. In contexts where states are captured by elites or actively dispossess marginalized communities, strengthening state capacity through adaptation planning may entrench the very structures producing vulnerability.

The geographical distribution of substantive topics—mountain concerns concentrated in Eastern Europe, cyclones in Pacific islands—might appear as appropriate specialization. But notice how these remain minoritized (each under 10% of corpus) while procedural topics dominate universally. Local climate realities become secondary to institutional performance. This is what Li [@li2007] calls "rendering technical"—the transformation of complex political ecologies into standardized problems amenable to expert intervention.

The post-structural lens examines not just what topics appear but what forms of knowledge the topic structure itself permits or forecloses. The dominance of planning discourse—with its emphasis on mainstreaming, agreements, and progress—does not merely exclude certain content. It eliminates entire ways of knowing and responding to environmental change.

Santos [@santos2016] provides the concept of epistemicide—the murder of knowledge systems. The topic model reveals this process empirically. Where are the topics capturing indigenous environmental management, reciprocal labor systems, or spiritual relationships with territory? These cannot appear because they cannot be expressed in planning language. A community's ancestral practices for managing drought through ceremony and seed exchange has no topic—it is rendered literally unspeakable within the NAP framework.

The term "vulnerability" itself, though pervasive in the plans, never appears as a standalone topic. Instead, it is subsumed within procedural discussions. This reveals what Escobar [@escobar2018] identifies as a key mechanism of development discourse: the naturalization of conditions that are politically produced. Communities are assessed as vulnerable—requiring technical assistance to build resilience—rather than examining how colonialism, structural adjustment, and ongoing extraction produce their vulnerability.

Topic 7's emphasis on "rcp," "rainfal," "ensembl," "confid," "trend" appears to represent scientific grounding. Yet this technical modeling language performs what Foucault identified as power/knowledge—the production of subjects and objects through expert discourse. Communities with sophisticated observational knowledge accumulated over generations become objects requiring climate science. Their knowledge cannot constitute a topic because it lacks the proper technical vocabulary.

The temporal politics embedded in these topics demands attention. The forward-looking orientation—"progress," "trend," "medium" (term planning)—systematically excludes historical analysis. Paprocki [@paprocki2018] shows how this temporal framing enables continued extraction by deferring political struggle to an indefinite future of "resilience." The absence of topics addressing historical emissions, colonial extraction, or ongoing dispossession is not oversight but structural to adaptation planning's futural orientation.

## Where Do Plans Come From?

The statistical analysis reveals an unexpected pattern in how adaptation discourse varies across country groupings. Regional institutional categories show an average effect size of `r region_effect`, while geographical categories show `r geography_effect`. This suggests that membership in a World Bank region or development bank catchment area explains substantially more variance in adaptation discourse than sharing similar climate vulnerabilities such as small island status or landlocked geography. This section examines possible explanations for these patterns through different theoretical lenses.

From an institutional perspective, the stronger regional effects could indicate successful policy coordination through regional organizations. The difference between regional and geographical effects (`r region_effect` versus `r geography_effect`) might reflect the effectiveness of regional climate governance architectures. The Inter-American Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, African Development Bank, and other regional bodies have established comprehensive climate programs providing technical assistance, funding mechanisms, and knowledge platforms for adaptation planning. The `r region_effect` effect size could capture the beneficial standardization emerging from these shared institutional frameworks.

Within regions, particular patterns deserve attention. Europe and Central Asia shows the highest effect size at `r europe_central_asia_effect`, coupled with dominance of `r europe_central_asia_dom`. This exceptional convergence might reflect the European Union's sophisticated climate governance architecture, including the EU Adaptation Strategy, the Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, and detailed technical guidance from the European Environment Agency. The emphasis on mountain ecosystems in this region's top topics aligns with transboundary initiatives like the Alpine Convention and Carpathian Convention, suggesting successful regional coordination around shared geographical features.

South Asia's effect size of `r south_asia_effect`, the second highest among regions, could similarly reflect coordination through SAARC climate initiatives and the shared technical support from ICIMOD (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development). The prominence of office and institutional topics alongside mainstream planning suggests these countries have developed similar institutional architectures for adaptation governance. This convergence might facilitate regional learning and cooperation on transboundary climate challenges like glacial melt and monsoon variability.

Latin America and Caribbean countries show both high dominance (`r latin_america_caribbean_dom`) and moderate effect size (`r latin_america_caribbean_effect`), an interesting combination suggesting strong convergence around specific topics while maintaining some diversity. The emphasis on transit and island topics alongside mainstream planning could reflect the region's dual challenge of sea-level rise for Caribbean islands and infrastructure vulnerability in mainland countries. The Inter-American Development Bank's climate change strategy, with its emphasis on both mitigation and adaptation, might explain this particular configuration.

In contrast, the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping shows lower effect size (`r middle_east_north_africa_afghanistan_pakistan_effect`) despite moderate dominance (`r middle_east_north_africa_afghanistan_pakistan_dom`). This could reflect weaker regional institutional frameworks or greater heterogeneity in national contexts, from oil-rich Gulf states to conflict-affected countries. The prominence of RCP scenarios in their top topics suggests more emphasis on climate modeling, possibly due to extreme uncertainty about precipitation patterns in arid regions.

The income patterns present a complex configuration requiring careful interpretation. Low-income countries exhibit the highest effect size (`r low_income_effect`), suggesting remarkably strong within-group similarity. From an institutional perspective, this could indicate successful harmonization of approaches for countries facing similar capacity constraints. The Green Climate Fund's Readiness Programme, specifically designed to help low-income countries develop NAPs, might contribute to this convergence by providing standardized templates and technical support packages.

Upper-middle income countries show the lowest effect size (`r upper_middle_income_effect`), which institutional theory might interpret as evidence of successful capacity building. These countries have developed sufficient institutional strength to pursue diverse approaches while still maintaining coordination with global frameworks. They can afford to experiment, innovate, and adapt templates to local contexts. Lower-middle income countries fall between these extremes (`r lower_middle_income_effect`), suggesting a transition zone where countries begin developing autonomous capacity while still relying on external support.

The non-linear pattern—with high-income countries at `r high_income_effect`—presents an interesting puzzle. These countries show more convergence than upper-middle income countries, possibly because they are establishing the templates and standards that others follow. Their discourse convergence might reflect consensus among donor countries about appropriate adaptation frameworks rather than constraint.

An alternative interpretation, drawing on Ferguson's [@ferguson1994] analysis of development discourse in Lesotho, might focus on how these patterns reflect power relations rather than successful coordination. Ferguson demonstrated how development interventions systematically depoliticize complex social issues by rendering them technical problems amenable to expert solutions. The gap between regional and geographical effects (`r region_effect` - `r geography_effect` = `r round(region_effect - geography_effect, 4)`) could indicate that adaptation planning operates similarly, responding more to institutional requirements than environmental realities.

The development apparatus Ferguson studied created what he called an "anti-politics machine"—transforming questions about poverty and inequality into technical issues about project management and service delivery. The regional effect of `r region_effect` might capture a similar process in climate adaptation. Regional development banks and UN agencies create standardized frameworks specifying how countries should assess vulnerability, identify adaptation options, and structure implementation plans. Countries within the same regional institution converge not necessarily through learning but through compliance with shared templates required for accessing climate finance.

Consider the concrete mechanisms producing regional convergence. The World Bank's Climate Change Knowledge Portal provides standardized data and assessment tools organized by region. The NAP Global Support Programme, implemented by UNDP and UNEP, operates through regional hubs that disseminate similar methodologies across neighboring countries. Regional climate funds have specific requirements and formats for project proposals. These institutional mechanisms could produce the observed regional effects independent of actual knowledge sharing or collaborative learning.

Li's [@li2007] concept of "rendering technical" offers another lens for interpreting the income patterns. Li showed how development interventions in Indonesia systematically translated complex political and social issues into technical problems with technical solutions. Low-income countries' high effect size (`r low_income_effect`) might reflect a similar process where diverse adaptation challenges are rendered into standardized technical categories. These countries may have limited capacity to resist or modify the frameworks that come bundled with technical assistance. They must express drought as meteorological anomaly rather than consequence of land dispossession, or frame flooding as infrastructure deficit rather than result of watershed deforestation driven by export agriculture.

The lower effect size for upper-middle income countries (`r upper_middle_income_effect`) could indicate greater ability to maintain complexity in their adaptation planning. With more resources and technical capacity, these countries might resist the simplification inherent in standardized frameworks. They can afford to hire local consultants who understand context, maintain parallel planning processes that capture local knowledge, or negotiate modifications to global templates. Lower-middle income countries' intermediate position (`r lower_middle_income_effect`) might reflect partial autonomy—able to adapt some elements while constrained to accept others.

The temporal patterns—increasing from `r early_effect` (early) to `r middle_effect` (middle) before slightly declining to `r late_effect` (late)—might reflect what Scott [@scott1998] describes as the state's effort to make society legible for governance. Scott demonstrated how states simplify complex realities into standardized categories that enable administration but lose crucial local knowledge. Early NAP adopters maintained more diversity (`r early_effect` effect size) as frameworks were still emerging and countries experimented with different approaches. By the middle period (`r middle_effect`), templates had solidified and countries converged around established formats that donors recognized and funded. The slight decline in the late period could reflect either innovation as frameworks mature or fatigue with existing approaches.

The extraordinarily high effect sizes for certain regions demand structural explanation. Europe and Central Asia's `r europe_central_asia_effect` effect size—the highest in the dataset—might indicate not successful coordination but complete capture by EU climate frameworks. Countries seeking EU accession or partnership must align their climate policies with the acquis communautaire. This creates powerful incentives for convergence that have little to do with shared climate vulnerabilities or collaborative learning.

A post-structural reading might examine how these patterns reflect deeper epistemological dynamics. Santos [@santos2016] argues that Western modernity operates through what he calls epistemicide—the systematic elimination of knowledge systems that don't conform to dominant frameworks. The `r round(region_effect - geography_effect, 4)` difference between regional and geographical effects could be read as measuring this process, where place-based knowledge about environmental change developed over generations is replaced by standardized planning frameworks developed in Washington, Geneva, or regional headquarters.

The variation in regional effect sizes might indicate different degrees of epistemological homogenization. Europe and Central Asia's extreme `r europe_central_asia_effect` effect size could suggest near-complete convergence around particular ways of understanding adaptation—vulnerability as measurable index, resilience as infrastructure investment, adaptation as sectoral mainstreaming. South Asia's similarly high `r south_asia_effect` might reflect the dominance of particular knowledge institutions like TERI (The Energy and Resources Institute) or ICIMOD that shape regional discourse through training programs, research collaborations, and technical assistance.

Sub-Saharan Africa's moderate effect size (`r sub_saharan_africa_effect`) presents an interesting case. Despite strong regional institutions like the African Development Bank and African Union, the region maintains more discourse diversity. This could reflect the persistence of alternative knowledge systems—indigenous environmental management, customary governance institutions, oral traditions about environmental variability. It might also indicate that regional institutions have less capacity to enforce convergence or that the diversity of contexts (from Sahelian drylands to Congo rainforests) resists standardization.

The income gradient could be interpreted through Mignolo's [@mignolo2000] concept of the coloniality of knowledge—how colonial relations persist through knowledge hierarchies that privilege Western ways of knowing. Low-income countries' `r low_income_effect` effect size might indicate not just financial dependency but epistemological subordination. These countries must translate their understanding of environmental change into categories legible to donors: seasonal flooding becomes "maladaptation," pastoral mobility becomes "forced migration," crop diversity becomes "climate-smart agriculture." The violence lies not in explicit prohibition but in the necessity of translation that loses meaning.

The lower effect sizes for middle-income countries could reflect what Chakrabarty [@chakrabarty2000] calls "provincializing Europe"—the capacity to maintain alternative knowledge frameworks alongside required international categories. Upper-middle income countries (`r upper_middle_income_effect` effect size) might have sufficient resources to support parallel knowledge systems: traditional agricultural calendars alongside climate models, indigenous territorial management alongside ecosystem-based adaptation, customary water sharing alongside integrated water resource management. They can afford the luxury of epistemological plurality.

High-income countries' moderate effect size (`r high_income_effect`) requires different interpretation. These countries don't face epistemological subordination but rather participate in creating the dominant frameworks. Their convergence might reflect what Escobar [@escobar2018] identifies as the reproduction of One World World (OWW) ontology—the assumption that there is one world knowable through science and manageable through planning. They converge because they share this fundamental onto-epistemological commitment, not because they're forced to adopt it.

Examining the concrete practices of plan production helps explain how these patterns emerge. National Adaptation Plans rarely emerge from purely national processes. They typically involve international funding (Green Climate Fund, bilateral donors), technical assistance (UNDP, UNEP, FAO), and consultant support (international firms, regional experts). Each element contributes to convergence patterns.

Regional development banks play crucial roles beyond funding. The Asian Development Bank's Climate Change and Disaster Risk Management Division doesn't just provide loans but offers technical assistance packages including consultant services, training programs, and knowledge products. When ADB supports NAP development in Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam, it often deploys the same consultants, uses the same vulnerability assessment tools, and applies the same economic analysis frameworks. The `r east_asia_pacific_effect` effect size for East Asia and Pacific partly emerges from these shared material practices.

The consultant economy deserves particular attention. International consulting firms like PwC, McKinsey, Arup, and AECOM have climate adaptation practices that operate across regions. A consultant based in Bangkok might work on plans for multiple Southeast Asian countries, carrying templates, frameworks, and language across borders. Regional consulting firms emerge to serve specific development bank territories. The stronger regional than geographical effects might partly reflect the geographical organization of consulting markets.

Bierschenk et al.'s [@bierschenk2002] concept of development brokers illuminates these dynamics. Consultants don't simply transfer knowledge; they translate between local contexts and international frameworks. But this translation is fundamentally asymmetric. Local knowledge must be translated into international categories to access resources, while international frameworks are rarely translated into local epistemologies. The broker's skill lies in making local realities legible to donors while maintaining sufficient local legitimacy.

The income patterns might reflect different modes of consultant engagement. Low-income countries' high effect size (`r low_income_effect`) could indicate heavy reliance on international consultants who apply standard templates with minimal modification. These consultants, paid by donors, have incentives to produce plans that satisfy donor requirements rather than capture local complexity. They know what triggers funding: proper vulnerability assessments, gender mainstreaming, ecosystem-based approaches, results frameworks. The plans converge because they're written for the same audience using the same tools.

Middle-income countries might engage consultants differently. With more resources, they can hire local firms or individual experts who understand context. They might use international consultants for specific technical inputs while maintaining national control over narrative and priorities. Upper-middle income countries' low effect size (`r upper_middle_income_effect`) could reflect this hybrid approach—meeting international requirements while preserving national perspectives.

These patterns suggest that adaptation planning discourse emerges from complex interactions between institutional requirements, power relations, knowledge hierarchies, and material practices. The stronger regional than geographical effects indicate that bureaucratic organization shapes discourse more than environmental realities. This raises questions about whether plans address actual adaptation needs or primarily serve institutional purposes.

The income patterns reveal how financial resources translate into discourse autonomy. Low-income countries' high effect size suggests limited ability to shape their own adaptation narratives. This constraint operates not through explicit prohibition but through the soft power of templates, technical assistance, and funding requirements. Middle-income countries' greater discourse diversity might indicate that economic development enables not just technical capacity but epistemological autonomy.

The regional variations hint at different models of knowledge production and circulation. Europe's extreme convergence might reflect dense networks of expertise and strong institutional frameworks, but also possibly limited epistemological diversity. Sub-Saharan Africa's moderate convergence could indicate either weaker institutional coordination or greater persistence of alternative knowledge systems. These differences matter for understanding whose knowledge shapes adaptation planning.

The temporal evolution suggests that adaptation planning might be undergoing standardization similar to other development interventions. The increase in effect sizes from early to middle periods could indicate the solidification of templates and frameworks. Whether the slight decline in the late period represents innovation or fatigue remains unclear. This trajectory raises concerns about path dependency—once frameworks are established, they become difficult to change even if they prove inadequate.

Understanding who shapes adaptation discourse becomes crucial for assessing plan effectiveness and legitimacy. If plans emerge primarily from consultant templates and regional institutional requirements rather than national deliberation and local knowledge, this might limit their relevance for actual adaptation needs. The patterns suggest both dynamics operate simultaneously, with the balance depending on income level, regional context, and temporal period. The question then becomes whether current planning processes can produce the kind of locally grounded, politically engaged responses that effective adaptation might require.
